s07 — structural variants as a confounder (chr19; the hard limit)

gwct

08/11/2026 21:49 EDT

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr)
source("analyses/lib/design.r")   # bartheme(), corecol(); knit from the project root

1 Question & design

Structural variants are where the whole framework breaks. Everything up to here treated reference bias as a function of divergence — how different the sample is, base for base. An SV is not that: a deletion removes reference-orthologous sequence, an insertion adds sequence with no reference home. It is unmappability, not high local divergence, so the separable divergence model (s05) does not describe it.

And there are two hard facts:

  • Our callers cannot call SVs. gatk / bcftools / freebayes are small-variant callers; they do not emit large deletions/insertions. So SVs are a ~100 % blind spot, and because iteration only bakes in what gets called, iteration cannot recover them either.
  • SVs still wreck the neighborhood. Reads spanning a breakpoint clip or fail to map, so small-variant recovery collapses locally around every SV.

This section measures SVs purely as a confounder of small-variant calling (recovering the SVs themselves would need dedicated SV callers + SV-aware scoring — out of scope).

  • Setup. 1000 homozygous SVs (~500 deletions + ~500 insertions, 50–5000 bp, uniform; insertions get random novel sequence) placed in the truth alongside a low SNP+indel background (D = 0.02) — low on purpose, so baseline small-variant recovery is high (~99 %) and the SV footprint stands out. Simulated (mason), mapped (bwa), called by all three callers, iterated with the s02 indel+liftover pipeline (workflow.smk, config-sv.yaml). chr19, 30×, seed 42.
  • Measurement (scripts/sv_confounder.py): every divergent SNP/indel truth site is binned by its distance to the nearest SV breakpoint (deletions contribute both junctions, insertions their anchor), and we score recovery (matched to the accumulated recovered set) per caller × iteration. The far bin (> 5 kb) is the SV-free baseline.
sv <- read_csv("analyses/s07-svs/results/s07-sv-confounder.csv") %>%
  mutate(caller = factor(caller, levels = c("gatk", "bcftools", "freebayes")),
         iteration = factor(iteration),
         dist_mid = as.numeric(dist_mid))
fp <- read_csv("analyses/s07-svs/results/s07-sv-confounder-fp.csv") %>%
  mutate(caller = factor(caller, levels = c("gatk", "bcftools", "freebayes")))
cols_it <- corecol(pal = "wilke", numcol = 3)

2 The SV footprint on small-variant recovery

SNP recovery against distance from the nearest SV breakpoint (log scale; the rightmost point is the > 5 kb baseline). Every caller has a hole at the breakpoint that heals within ~one read length — but the depth of the hole is a caller property.

d <- sv %>% filter(vtype == "snp", bptype == "any")
ggplot(d, aes(dist_mid, recall, color = iteration)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols_it, name = "iteration") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  facet_wrap(~caller, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "distance to nearest SV breakpoint (bp, log scale; last point = >5 kb baseline)",
       y = "SNP recall") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Interpretation.

  • The pileup callers lose ~10 points at the breakpoint (bcftools/freebayes 0.89 vs ~0.98 baseline, 0–50 bp) and heal by ~100 bp — only the reads that span the junction clip; the clean flanking reads still call the nearby SNP.
  • gatk loses ~40 points (0.58 vs 0.97 baseline). Its reassembler is confounded by the clipped/chimeric reads at the junction and fails to assemble the local haplotype — the same calling-limited vulnerability seen throughout (s05), now triggered by SV breakpoints rather than divergence.
  • Iteration lifts the neighborhood but cannot close the breakpoint. From iteration 1 → 3 the hole shrinks a little (gatk 0.58 → 0.64 at 0–50 bp) but a large residual remains, because the SV is never called, never baked into the consensus, so breakpoint-spanning reads keep clipping at every iteration. The dropout right at the junction is permanent.

2.1 Deletions vs. insertions

Splitting by the type of the nearest breakpoint (iteration 1). Both punch a hole; insertions are marginally worse at the junction (fully unmappable novel sequence vs a deletion junction whose flanking reads still partly map).

di <- sv %>% filter(vtype == "snp", bptype %in% c("del", "ins"), iteration == "1")
ggplot(di, aes(dist_mid, recall, color = bptype)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = corecol(pal = "wilke", numcol = 2),
                     name = NULL, labels = c(del = "deletion", ins = "insertion")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  facet_wrap(~caller, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "distance to nearest SV breakpoint (bp, log scale)", y = "SNP recall (iteration 1)") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

3 SVs also create false positives near breakpoints

The other side of the confounder: clipped/chimeric reads at breakpoints don’t just lose true calls, they spawn false ones. Enrichment = the fraction of a caller’s single-shot false positives within 150 bp of a breakpoint, divided by the genomic fraction that close (0.74 %).

ggplot(fp, aes(caller, enrichment, fill = caller)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f×\n(%d FPs)", enrichment, n_fp)), vjust = -0.2, size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = corecol(pal = "wilke", numcol = 3), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "FP enrichment within 150 bp of a breakpoint (× genomic)") +
  bartheme()

Interpretation. gatk (2.6×) and bcftools (1.7×) concentrate false positives at breakpoints — the chimeric reads there generate spurious calls. freebayes is the exception (0.7×) not because it’s clean but the opposite: it emits so many false positives everywhere (231 k, its complex/multiallelic floor from s02) that breakpoints don’t stand out. So SVs degrade precision locally for the disciplined callers, and freebayes’ FP problem swamps the signal.

4 The blind spot

Of the 1000 SVs, the number recovered by small-variant calling + iteration is 0 (bcftools, gatk) or 1 (freebayes, an incidental large complex call — not systematic SV recovery). SVs are, by construction, invisible to this pipeline: the callers can’t emit them and iteration can’t bake in what was never called. This is the permanent blind spot — no amount of divergence-recovery machinery touches it.

5 Summary

  • SVs are off the divergence axis. They are unmappability, not high local divergence, so the separable model (s05) does not describe them — this is where the framework stops.
  • A sharp local footprint on small-variant recovery. SNP recovery craters within ~50 bp of a breakpoint and heals by ~100 bp. The depth is caller-specific: pileup callers −10 pt, gatk −40 pt (its reassembler fails on the junction reads — the calling-limited mechanism again).
  • Iteration can’t close it. It lifts the neighborhood slightly but the breakpoint dropout is permanent, because the SV is never called and so never enters the consensus.
  • Precision suffers too. False positives are enriched 1.7–2.6× at breakpoints for the disciplined callers (freebayes’ baseline FP flood hides it).
  • The SVs themselves are a ~100 % blind spot. Small-variant calling + iteration recover essentially none of them.
  • Bottom line — the hard limit. Reference bias from SNPs and indels is a recall problem that mapping quality and iteration can push back on. SVs are a different failure mode: a permanent, local blind spot that iterative small-variant calling cannot address, only avoid. Recovering them needs dedicated SV callers — a separate problem.

Data tables + dictionaries: results/s07-sv-confounder.csv (recovery vs distance) and results/s07-sv-confounder-fp.csv (FP enrichment). SVs on a D = 0.02 background, single seed 42.
